newsitem.title: USA: High-powered consulting for entrepreneurs -- for free.
newsitem.headline: High-powered consulting for entrepreneurs -- for free.

text.p: Here's a no-brainer for you: you're looking for someone to advise you on turning your idea for a business into a going concern.
You might hire a private consultant. But you also could tap into a nationwide network of experienced business executives who also happen to offer their services free of charge.
This is one case where the old adage that "You get what you pay for" does not necessarily ring true.

The Service Corps of Retired Executives, better known as SCORE, offers one-on-one counselling and mentoring to owners of small businesses. It has 12,400 retired and still-working executives and business owners who volunteer as counsellors in 389 chapters across the country, as well as in Guam and Puerto Rico.

In June, the group launched a Web site (http://www.score.org) that offers 24-hour access to about 150 counsellors in numerous locations via e-mail, as well 150 pages of content on its services and links to other business information sites.

The Web site also helps entrepreneurs find the location of the nearest SCORE office. Or you can call 800-634-0245 for referral to the nearest chapter, which will arrange an initial interview with a counsellor who will work with you on an ongoing basis.
The group also runs workshops on specific business issues, sponsored by local chapters. They are generally offered free or for a nominal fee.

"There are lots of people who have a potentially good idea or skill on which a small business can be based," said Fred Thomas, SCORE president. "What they often lack is the understanding that an entrepreneur has to be able to produce the product, figure out pricing, market it, etc -- beyond just having a good product. That lack of appreciation causes a lot of people to stumble and do less planning than they really should."

SCORE's executive director, Ken Yancey, says new business owners do themselves a disservice if they don't take advantage of the group's counsellors. "They offer an opportunity to have a third party that's not family and doesn't have a stake in the business.

"They act as a sounding board, an advice-giver," he said. "So many small business owners don't have the opportunity to talk to someone else. Here, they get the benefit of experience. That's the type of experience that provides the wisdom and understanding that's so beneficial to a small business owner."

SCORE counsellors' business experiences are varied. About 20 percent to 30 percent come from a small-business background, depending on the region. Others, like Thomas, have worked for high-powered consulting firms such as McKinsey & Co. or been executives with corporate giants like Citicorp or General Electric Co.

"Most of our people are characterised by their willingness to continue to learn what's relevant," said Thomas. "Frankly, I, and many others who came out of the corporate culture, had some learning to do regarding what was needed to advise small business owners."

The group recognises that some new entrepreneurs might be intimidated by the prospect of bringing their ideas to such business veterans. "We try to instill in our counsellors that people might feel a little intimidated and prepare them for that," said Thomas. "We want them to come back and work with us on a continuing basis."

The group has a professional development programme for counsellors that lasts about 6 months. "They all go through the same drill," said Thomas. "When someone joins a chapter, we link them to a mentor to make sure they have the basic training, make sure they understand the code of ethics and attend workshops."
A first session between counsellor and client often is just getting to understand each other -- getting clear on what the issues are and starting the client on organising needed information.

SCORE uses a 20-page workbook/brochure on starting a business that was compiled with Inc. magazine and Apple Computer Inc. It covers issues ranging from testing and protecting a business idea to finding money, cash flow and developing a business plan.
"It has all the elements of a business plan," said Yancey. "It's an excellent piece that puts people on the right track. They can go through that process with a SCORE counsellor aiding them."

The group recommends that would-be entrepreneurs keep their day jobs until they've completed their investigative, planning and financial analyses. It also encourages people to work in the industry they're thinking of entering.

"When they have an idea of the potential of the business, they need to ask themselves whether they want to take the risk," said Thomas. "There are lots of people who do and end up making a lot more money than they would if they stayed in corporate employment.
"But there are also a lot who end up between a rock and a hard place."

One thing the group keeps track of is how many sessions a counsellor has with a particular client. "Most of the success stories involved 40, 50, or 60 sessions," said Thomas. "We're very keen on emphasising that it's a long-term relationship."
